extracted.intended_audience: students and readers interested in the history of early American journalism and newspapers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and descriptive standards the chapter uses to characterize, evaluate, and explain early (late-17th to mid-18th century) American newspapers: their formats, content choices, editorial policies, economic models, legal constraints, and journalistic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical format and frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspaper ... was on what the printers called a half-sheet; it consisted of a single leaf ... printed on both sides, and issued weekly. Sometimes Campbell grew ambitious and printed three or four pages; he advertised that those who wanted his 'Letter of Intelligence' on a full sheet of writing paper with two pages left blank for correspondence might have it in that format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format (half-sheet vs full sheet), number of pages (one leaf, two pages, four pages, six pages), and frequency (weekly, every other week, occasional increases) were defining production choices. Offering subscription options (full sheet with blank pages) was a product differentiation strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content mix — foreign vs local news
rubrics_metrics.description: Editor Campbell ... filled about two-thirds of his paper with news taken from London journals ... The remainder of an average issue was filled with items ... about the arrival of ships, deaths, sermons, political appointments, storms, Indian depredations, privateering and piracies, counterfeiting, fires, accidents, court actions, and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear balance between reprinted foreign/English intelligence and concise local items was standard; the proportion and selection shaped reader utility and identity of the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maritime news as a staple
rubrics_metrics.description: Maritime news was always of importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given colonial dependence on shipping, arrivals, ship movements, privateering, and piracy were high-value items and regularly prioritized in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest and circumstantial reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Too seldom was found the kind of circumstantial, human-interest story that gives life to the dry bones of the news— like one from the Piscataqua (Portsmouth) correspondent ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human-interest, eyewitness, or circumstantial narratives enlivened otherwise sparse reporting; their absence made early papers seem unexciting to modern readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensational stories
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper’s most sensational news, on the whole, was that which dealt with pirates and piracies, and one of the best stories published ... was the account of how the pirate 'Blackbeard' (Teach) was slain ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensational or dramatic incidents could be the most attention-getting items and were important for circulation and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness vs considering news as 'recent history'
rubrics_metrics.description: Campbell’s theory of the presentation of foreign news gave little consideration to timeliness. Boston was some two months away from England ... Campbell thought of news as recent history. But by reason of his meager space and his suspensions, he got further and further behind in his record ... By 1718 he was more than a year behind ... he now intends to make up that Deficiency by Printing a Sheet ... every other Week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness was a developing standard: being current mattered for perceived value; delays or backlog ('recent history' becoming 'ancient history') reduced relevance and forced production changes (more pages, more frequent issues) to catch up.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Published by Authority' and government approval
rubrics_metrics.description: The News-Letter carried a line under its name-plate attesting to the fact that it was 'Published by Authority.' This meant that the Governor or his secretary commonly approved the contents of the paper before printing;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Published by Authority' signaled official supervision/censorship. It affected editorial content, risk of rebuke, and sometimes brought subsidies; it was both a protection and a constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship with authorities, censorship, and subsidies
rubrics_metrics.description: With the suppression of Publick Occurrences in his memory, and current examples of the prohibition of pamphlets and broadsides which gave offence coming to his attention, Campbell was shrewd enough to avoid serious difficulties with authority; indeed, small subsidies were paid him from the public treasury in the early years of the News-Letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cautious relationship with government could secure material support and avoid reprisals; defiance of authorities could provoke rebuke, imprisonment, or legal orders restricting publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence vs official supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: The Courant ... was not 'published by authority,' but rather in spite of it. It had no connection with the post-office, gave comparatively small attention to news, and carried very little advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent editorial stance enabled trenchant criticism, satire, and entertainment-focused journalism, but increased legal and political risk and could affect advertising/revenue profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment and literary essays as a newspaper function
rubrics_metrics.description: It took for its model, not the London Gazette, but such literary essay-papers as the Spectator and Guardian. It was less anxious to be informative than to be amusing ... The main Design of this Weekly Paper will be to entertain the Town with the most comical and diverting Incidents of Humane Life ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers could position themselves as entertainers (essays, satire, witty pieces) rather than strictly informational organs; this function broadened the role of journalism to include literary and social commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of satire, impersonation, and pseudonymous essays
rubrics_metrics.description: His writers satirized pretending learning, religious hypocrisy ... Ben stuck his first essay under the door ... This was the first of the 'Dogood Papers' ... fairly close imitations ... of Addison’s Spectator papers, but they dealt with Boston characters and Boston questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire, pseudonymous personas, and imitation of popular literary models were accepted rhetorical tools to critique society and attract readership, but could antagonize powerful targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical limits: one-sided crusades and personal attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: This first American newspaper crusade did what such campaigns still do; it won the attention of the town, gave a one-sided story, and built circulation, and it made the paper bitter enemies. But it did not accomplish the purpose which alone justifies such efforts ethically: it did not win support for a good cause. The Courant was wrong in the first place. It fought against a beneficent reform, and it used personal attacks in its fight;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaign journalism may build circulation but risks ethical failings if it is one-sided, uses personal attacks, or is directed against beneficial reforms; ethical justification requires substantial, defensible aims and fair methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising and revenue patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: A few advertisements usually appeared at the bottom of the last column ... Draper’s paper ... well printed, crammed with advertising, and carrying a respectable quota of news ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising placement and volume were key revenue sources; increased advertising correlated with larger, more sustainable papers and influenced layout and page allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription price and perceived luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: The subscription price of the News-Letter was twopence a copy, or twelve shillings a year, delivered. That it was considered a luxury is illustrated by the fact that Judge Sewall occasionally presented copies of it to the ladies on whom he called ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Price relative to income determined market penetration; higher cost meant limited circulation and a more elite readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation, suspensions, and financial viability
rubrics_metrics.description: The News-Letter was suspended twice during its first six years, but it was revived after lapses of two and eight months, respectively. After seven years of publication Campbell complained that he could not 'vend 250 copies at one impression.' ... the publisher now 'cannot vend 300 copies at an impression'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interruption of publication, low sales figures, and inability to sustain impressions were primary measures of commercial failure; expansion of pages or frequency were attempted remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of correspondents and news-gathering reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Campbell had correspondents at several important points, though they were neither regular nor efficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having correspondents extended coverage but irregular, unreliable contributions limited depth and timeliness; organization of correspondent networks influenced news quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page count and enlargement as a quality/competitiveness indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: Draper enlarged his paper until it consisted of four good-sized pages, and sometimes six, well printed, crammed with advertising, and carrying a respectable quota of news ... By printing every other Week a Sheet and this Month Weekly a Sheet, we have given you not only the Remarkable Occurrences of Great Britain and Ireland to the 4th of March last ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increasing page counts allowed more news, essays, and ads; enlargement was both a response to audience demand and a competitive strategy to reduce staleness and increase perceived value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial impartiality as an ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: The Evening-Post ... claimed to be impartial; and, except for its editor’s dislike of clergymen generally, it seems to have lived up to that ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claiming impartiality and actually maintaining balanced coverage was a recognized editorial standard that could enhance credibility and readership across factions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of feature articles and lively writing style
rubrics_metrics.description: Its feature articles were carefully selected, and its news was written with more wit and liveliness than that of most other colonial newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful curation of features plus engaging, witty prose were competitive editorial choices that improved reader appeal and differentiated papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political alignment, advocacy, and partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Draper’s News-Letter ... Its activities as a Royalist paper will be noticed later; it perished early in the Revolution ... the Pennsylvania Journal ... in the Revolutionary era it was to become a great Patriot organ ... The Courant was launched as an anti-inoculation paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers frequently took explicit political stances (Royalist, Patriot, anti-inoculation); alignment could build committed readership but also risk alienation, legal action, or demise depending on political developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal risk management and evasive practices
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Court took action 'That James Franklin be strictly forbidden by this Court to print or publish the New-England Courant or any Pamphlet or paper of the like Nature, Except it be first Supervised, by the Secretary of this Provinee.' In order to evade this order, James Franklin resorted to a trick: he canceled his brother’s apprenticeship indentures and substituted Benjamin’s name for his own in the 'imprint' of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printers used legal and procedural maneuvers (imprint substitution, revoking apprenticeships) to evade censorship orders; such practices highlight the interaction of law, commerce, and editorial survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of London models and use of reprints
rubrics_metrics.description: In appearance, and in some features of news treatment, the paper was not unlike the London Gazette. The Courant ... took for its model ... the Spectator and Guardian ... Many papers imitated London papers, just as those papers imitated each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitating successful London titles (Gazette, Spectator) and reprinting English content were normative practices shaping tone, format, and expectations of colonial readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market competition, consolidation, and town-level news ecology
rubrics_metrics.description: By 1735 there were five newspapers in Boston, a town which still had less than 20,000 population. This situation brought to pass the first American newspaper consolidation: the Journal publishers bought the old Gazette and merged their paper with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The number of papers in a market, competition for readers/ads, and consolidation events were structural determinants of content strategy, survival, and editorial positions.
